3193.name: sqlx_core
3193.docs:
Core of SQLx, the rust SQL toolkit.

### Note: Semver Exempt API
The API of this crate is not meant for general use and does *not* follow Semantic Versioning.
The only crate that follows Semantic Versioning in the project is the `sqlx` crate itself.
If you are building a custom SQLx driver, you should pin an exact version for `sqlx-core` to
avoid breakages:

189.name: async_stream
189.docs:
A minimalist clone of the `async-stream` crate in 100% safe code, without proc macros.

This was created initially to get around some weird compiler errors we were getting with
`async-stream`, and now it'd just be more work to replace.

Returned from [`Row::get`](crate::row::Row::get) if the value from the database is `NULL`,

The error kind.

This enum is to be used to identify frequent errors that can be handled by the program.
Although it currently only supports constraint violations, the type may grow in the future.

583.name: pool
583.docs:
Provides the connection pool for asynchronous SQLx connections.

Opening a database connection for each and every operation to the database can quickly
become expensive. Furthermore, sharing a database connection between threads and functions
can be difficult to express in Rust.

391.name: PoolConnection
391.docs:
A connection managed by a [`Pool`][crate::pool::Pool].

Will be returned to the pool on-drop.

430.name: close
430.docs:
Close this connection, allowing the pool to open a replacement.

Equivalent to calling [`.detach()`] then [`.close()`], but the connection permit is retained
for the duration so that the pool may not exceed `max_connections`.

431.name: close_on_drop
431.docs:
Close this connection on-drop, instead of returning it to the pool.

May be used in cases where waiting for the [`.close()`][Self::close] call
to complete is unacceptable, but you still want the connection to be closed gracefully
so that the server can clean up resources.

428.name: detach
428.docs:
Detach this connection from the pool, allowing it to open a replacement.

Note that if your application uses a single shared pool, this
effectively lets the application exceed the [`max_connections`] setting.

434.name: leak
434.docs:
Detach this connection from the pool, treating it as permanently checked-out.

This effectively will reduce the maximum capacity of the pool by 1 every time it is used.

520.name: PoolConnectionMetadata
520.docs: Metadata for the connection being processed by a [`PoolOptions`] callback.

497.name: PoolOptions
497.docs:
Configuration options for [`Pool`][super::Pool].

### Callback Functions: Why Do I Need `Box::pin()`?
Essentially, because it's impossible to write generic bounds that describe a closure
with a higher-ranked lifetime parameter, returning a future with that same lifetime.

498.name: new
498.docs:
Returns a default "sane" configuration, suitable for testing or light-duty applications.

Production applications will likely want to at least modify
[`max_connections`][Self::max_connections].

432.name: max_connections
432.docs:
Set the maximum number of connections that this pool should maintain.

Be mindful of the connection limits for your database as well as other applications
which may want to connect to the same database (or even multiple instances of the same
application in high-availability deployments).

499.name: get_max_connections
499.docs: Get the maximum number of connections that this pool should maintain

433.name: min_connections
433.docs:
Set the minimum number of connections to maintain at all times.

When the pool is built, this many connections will be automatically spun up.

502.name: get_min_connections
502.docs: Get the minimum number of connections to maintain at all times.

503.name: acquire_time_level
503.docs:
Enable logging of time taken to acquire a connection from the connection pool via
[`Pool::acquire()`].

If slow acquire logging is also enabled, this level is used for acquires that are not
considered slow.

505.name: acquire_slow_level
505.docs:
Log excessive time taken to acquire a connection at a different log level than time taken
for faster connection acquires via [`Pool::acquire()`].

506.name: acquire_slow_threshold
506.docs:
Set a threshold for reporting excessive time taken to acquire a connection from
the connection pool via [`Pool::acquire()`]. When the threshold is exceeded, a warning is logged.

Defaults to a value that should not typically be exceeded by the pool enlarging
itself with an additional new connection.

508.name: get_acquire_slow_threshold
508.docs:
Get the threshold for reporting excessive time taken to acquire a connection via
[`Pool::acquire()`].

512.name: acquire_timeout
512.docs:
Set the maximum amount of time to spend waiting for a connection in [`Pool::acquire()`].

Caps the total amount of time `Pool::acquire()` can spend waiting across multiple phases:

513.name: get_acquire_timeout
513.docs: Get the maximum amount of time to spend waiting for a connection in [`Pool::acquire()`].

500.name: max_lifetime
500.docs:
Set the maximum lifetime of individual connections.

Any connection with a lifetime greater than this will be closed.

514.name: get_max_lifetime
514.docs: Get the maximum lifetime of individual connections.

501.name: idle_timeout
501.docs:
Set a maximum idle duration for individual connections.

Any connection that remains in the idle queue longer than this will be closed.

515.name: get_idle_timeout
515.docs: Get the maximum idle duration for individual connections.

509.name: test_before_acquire
509.docs:
If true, the health of a connection will be verified by a call to [`Connection::ping`]
before returning the connection.

Defaults to `true`.

511.name: after_connect
511.docs:
Perform an asynchronous action after connecting to the database.

If the operation returns with an error then the error is logged, the connection is closed
and a new one is opened in its place and the callback is invoked again.

510.name: before_acquire
510.docs:
Perform an asynchronous action on a previously idle connection before giving it out.

 Alongside the connection, the closure gets [`PoolConnectionMetadata`] which contains
 potentially useful information such as the connection's age and the duration it was
 idle.

518.name: after_release
518.docs:
Perform an asynchronous action on a connection before it is returned to the pool.

Alongside the connection, the closure gets [`PoolConnectionMetadata`] which contains
potentially useful information such as the connection's age.

This ensures the configuration is correct.

522.name: connect_with

Create a new pool from this `PoolOptions` and immediately open at least one connection.

524.name: connect_lazy

Create a new pool from this `PoolOptions`, but don't open any connections right now.

525.name: connect_lazy_with

427.name: Pool
427.docs:
An asynchronous pool of SQLx database connections.

Create a pool with [Pool::connect] or [Pool::connect_with] and then call [Pool::acquire]
to get a connection from the pool; when the connection is dropped it will return to the pool
so it can be reused.

581.name: connect
581.docs:
Create a new connection pool with a default pool configuration and
the given connection URL, and immediately establish one connection.

Refer to the relevant `ConnectOptions` impl for your database for the expected URL format:

582.name: connect_with
582.docs:
Create a new connection pool with a default pool configuration and
the given `ConnectOptions`, and immediately establish one connection.

The default configuration is mainly suited for testing and light-duty applications.
For production applications, you'll likely want to make at least few tweaks.

587.name: connect_lazy
587.docs:
Create a new connection pool with a default pool configuration and
the given connection URL.

The pool will establish connections only as needed.

588.name: connect_lazy_with
588.docs:
Create a new connection pool with a default pool configuration and
the given `ConnectOptions`.

The pool will establish connections only as needed.

252.name: acquire
252.docs:
Retrieves a connection from the pool.

The total time this method is allowed to execute is capped by
[`PoolOptions::acquire_timeout`].
If that timeout elapses, this will return [`Error::PoolClosed`].

589.name: try_acquire
589.docs:
Attempts to retrieve a connection from the pool if there is one available.

Returns `None` immediately if there are no idle connections available in the pool
or there are tasks waiting for a connection which have yet to wake.

584.name: begin
584.docs: Retrieves a connection and immediately begins a new transaction.

590.name: try_begin
590.docs: Attempts to retrieve a connection and immediately begins a new transaction if successful.

591.name: begin_with
591.docs: Retrieves a connection and immediately begins a new transaction using `statement`.

592.name: try_begin_with
592.docs:
Attempts to retrieve a connection and, if successful, immediately begins a new
transaction using `statement`.

254.name: close
254.docs:
Shut down the connection pool, immediately waking all tasks waiting for a connection.

Upon calling this method, any currently waiting or subsequent calls to [`Pool::acquire`] and
the like will immediately return [`Error::PoolClosed`] and no new connections will be opened.
Checked-out connections are unaffected, but will be gracefully closed on-drop
rather than being returned to the pool.

593.name: is_closed
593.docs: Returns `true` if [`.close()`][Pool::close] has been called on the pool, `false` otherwise.

594.name: close_event
594.docs:
Get a future that resolves when [`Pool::close()`] is called.

If the pool is already closed, the future resolves immediately.

596.name: size
596.docs: Returns the number of connections currently active. This includes idle connections.

597.name: num_idle
597.docs: Returns the number of connections active and idle (not in use).

598.name: connect_options
598.docs: Gets a clone of the connection options for this pool

599.name: set_connect_options
599.docs:

existing open connection in the pool will be left as-is.

600.name: options
600.docs: Get the options for this pool

595.name: CloseEvent
595.docs:
A future that resolves when the pool is closed.

See [`Pool::close_event()`] for details.

641.name: do_until
641.docs:
Execute the given future until it returns or the pool is closed.

Cancels the future and returns `Err(PoolClosed)` if/when the pool is closed.
If the pool was already closed, the future is never run.

476.name: Transaction
476.docs:
An in-progress database transaction or savepoint.

A transaction starts with a call to [`Pool::begin`] or [`Connection::begin`].

1239.name: ColumnIndex
1239.docs:
A type that can be used to index into a [`Row`] or [`Statement`].

The [`get`] and [`try_get`] methods of [`Row`] accept any type that implements `ColumnIndex`.
This trait is implemented for strings which are used to look up a column by name, and for
`usize` which is used as a positional index into the row.

1237.name: Statement
1237.docs:
An explicitly prepared statement.

Statements are prepared and cached by default, per connection. This type allows you to
look at that cache in-between the statement being prepared and it being executed. This contains
the expected columns to be returned and the expected parameter types (if available).

1282.name: StatementCache
1282.docs:
A cache for prepared statements. When full, the least recently used
statement gets removed.

1283.name: new
1283.docs: Create a new cache with the given capacity.

1284.name: get_mut
1284.docs:

1285.name: insert
1285.docs:
Inserts a new statement to the cache, returning the least recently used
statement id if the cache is full, or if inserting with an existing key,
the replaced existing statement.

1286.name: len
1286.docs: The number of statements in the cache.

1288.name: remove_lru
1288.docs: Removes the least recently used item from the cache.

1289.name: clear
1289.docs: Clear all cached statements from the cache.

1290.name: contains_key
1290.docs: True if cache has a value for the given key.

1291.name: capacity
1291.docs: Returns the maximum number of statements the cache can hold.

1292.name: is_enabled
1292.docs: Returns true if the cache capacity is more than 0.

Note, however, that with Postgres you can get much better performance by using arrays

1935.name: fetch
1935.docs: Execute the query and return the generated results as a stream.

1936.name: fetch_many
1936.docs:
Execute multiple queries and return the generated results as a stream
from each query, in a stream.

1937.name: fetch_all
1937.docs:
Execute the query and return all the resulting rows collected into a [`Vec`].

### Note: beware result set size.
This will attempt to collect the full result set of the query into memory.

1938.name: fetch_one
1938.docs:
Execute the query, returning the first row or [`Error::RowNotFound`] otherwise.

### Note: for best performance, ensure the query returns at most one row.
Depending on the driver implementation, if your query can return more than one row,
it may lead to wasted CPU time and bandwidth on the database server.

1939.name: fetch_optional
1939.docs:
Execute the query, returning the first row or `None` otherwise.

### Note: for best performance, ensure the query returns at most one row.
Depending on the driver implementation, if your query can return more than one row,
it may lead to wasted CPU time and bandwidth on the database server.

1930.name: query_scalar
1930.docs:
Execute a single SQL query as a prepared statement (transparently cached) and extract the first
column of each row.

Extracts the first column of each row. Additional columns are ignored.
Any type that implements `Type<DB> + Decode<DB>` may be used.

1959.name: query_scalar_with
1959.docs:
Execute a SQL query as a prepared statement (transparently cached), with the given arguments,
and extract the first column of each row.

See [`query_scalar()`] for details.

1960.name: query_scalar_with_result
1960.docs: Same as [`query_scalar_with`] but takes arguments as Result

1430.name: RawSql
1430.docs:
One or more raw SQL statements, separated by semicolons (`;`).

See [`raw_sql()`] for details.

1966.name: execute
1966.docs: Execute the SQL string and return the total number of rows affected.

1967.name: execute_many
1967.docs: Execute the SQL string. Returns a stream which gives the number of rows affected for each statement in the string.

1968.name: fetch
1968.docs:
Execute the SQL string and return the generated results as a stream.

If the string contains multiple statements, their results will be concatenated together.

1969.name: fetch_many
1969.docs:
Execute the SQL string and return the generated results as a stream.

For each query in the stream, any generated rows are returned first,
then the `QueryResult` with the number of rows affected.

1970.name: fetch_all
1970.docs:
Execute the SQL string and return all the resulting rows collected into a [`Vec`].

### Note: beware result set size.
This will attempt to collect the full result set of the query into memory.

1971.name: fetch_one
1971.docs:
Execute the SQL string, returning the first row or [`Error::RowNotFound`] otherwise.

### Note: for best performance, ensure the query returns at most one row.
Depending on the driver implementation, if your query can return more than one row,
it may lead to wasted CPU time and bandwidth on the database server.

1973.name: fetch_optional
1973.docs:
Execute the SQL string, returning the first row or [`None`] otherwise.

### Note: for best performance, ensure the query returns at most one row.
Depending on the driver implementation, if your query can return more than one row,
it may lead to wasted CPU time and bandwidth on the database server.

1965.name: raw_sql
1965.docs:
Execute one or more statements as raw SQL, separated by semicolons (`;`).

This interface can be used to execute both DML
(Data Manipulation Language: `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and variants)
as well as DDL (Data Definition Language: `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, etc).

1236.name: Row
1236.docs:
Represents a single row from the database.

[`FromRow`]: crate::row::FromRow
[`Query::fetch`]: crate::query::Query::fetch

2133.name: ParamChecking
2133.docs: The type of query parameter checking done by a SQL database.

2164.name: TypeChecking
2164.docs:
Type-checking extensions for the `Database` trait.

Mostly supporting code for the macros, and for `Debug` impls.

2163.name: FmtValue
2163.docs: An adapter for [`Value`] which attempts to decode the value and format it when printed using [`Debug`].

2167.name: debug
2167.docs:
When printed with [`Debug`], attempt to decode `value` as the given type `T` and format it using [`Debug`].

If `value` could not be decoded as `T`, the reason is printed instead.

2168.name: unknown
2168.docs:
If the type to be decoded is not known or not supported, print the SQL type instead,
as well as any applicable SQLx feature that needs to be enabled.

1353.name: TypeInfo
1353.docs: Provides information about a SQL type for the database driver.

1355.name: Value
1355.docs: An owned value from the database.

1356.name: ValueRef
1356.docs: A reference to a single value from the database.

2302.name: MigrationType
2302.docs: Migration Type represents the type of migration

2370.name: Migrator
2370.docs:
A resolved set of migrations, ready to be run.

Can be constructed statically using `migrate!()` or at runtime using [`Migrator::new()`].

2405.name: new
2405.docs:
Creates a new instance with the given source.

# Examples

2407.name: set_ignore_missing
2407.docs: Specify whether applied migrations that are missing from the resolved migrations should be ignored.

2408.name: set_locking
2408.docs:
Specify whether or not to lock the database during migration. Defaults to `true`.

### Warning
Disabling locking can lead to errors or data loss if multiple clients attempt to apply migrations simultaneously
without some sort of mutual exclusion.

2409.name: iter
2409.docs: Get an iterator over all known migrations.

2411.name: version_exists
2411.docs: Check if a migration version exists.

2412.name: run
2412.docs:
Run any pending migrations against the database; and, validate previously applied migrations
against the current migration source to detect accidental changes in previously-applied migrations.

# Examples

2413.name: undo
2413.docs:
Run down migrations against the database until a specific version.

# Examples

2406.name: MigrationSource
2406.docs:
In the default implementation, a MigrationSource is a directory which
contains the migration SQL scripts. All these scripts must be stored in
files with names using the format `<VERSION>_<DESCRIPTION>.sql`, where
`<VERSION>` is a string that can be parsed into `i64` and its value is
greater than zero, and `<DESCRIPTION>` is a string.

Files that don't match this format are silently ignored.

1380.name: any
1380.docs:
**SEE DOCUMENTATION BEFORE USE**. Generic database driver with the specific driver selected at runtime.

The underlying database drivers are chosen at runtime from the list set via
[`install_drivers`][self::driver::install_drivers]. Any use of `AnyConnection` or `AnyPool`
without this will panic.

2838.name: types
2838.docs:
Conversions between Rust and standard **SQL** types.

# Types

2990.name: install_drivers
2990.docs:
Install the list of drivers for [`AnyConnection`] to use.

Must be called before an `AnyConnection` or `AnyPool` can be connected.

697.name: AnyConnection
697.docs:
A connection to _any_ SQLx database.

The database driver used is determined by the scheme
of the connection url.

2547.name: backend_name
2547.docs: Returns the name of the database backend in use (e.g. PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, etc.)

354.name: Any
354.docs:
Opaque database driver. Capable of being used in place of any SQLx database driver. The actual
driver used will be selected at runtime, from the connection url.

688.name: AnyConnectOptions
688.docs:
Opaque options for connecting to a database. These may only be constructed by parsing from
a connection url.

3015.name: FixtureSnapshot
3015.docs:
A snapshot of the current state of the database.

Can be used to generate an `INSERT` fixture for populating an empty database,
or in the future it may be possible to generate a fixture from the difference between
two snapshots.

3016.name: additive_fixture
3016.docs:
Generate a fixture to reproduce this snapshot from an empty database using `INSERT`s.

Note that this doesn't take into account any triggers that might modify the data before
it's stored.

3166.name: driver_prelude
3166.docs:
Helper module to get drivers compiling again that used to be in this crate,
to avoid having to replace tons of `use crate::<...>` imports.

This module can be glob-imported and should not clash with any modules a driver
would want to implement itself.
